title: The Gospels and the Parables
bigQuestion: How do four different books, written decades after the events, tell one story of Jesus that Christians still read as good news?

story.title: The Story on the Ashland Bus
story.kicker: A tired rider retells a two-thousand-year-old story to a bored nephew, and the whole back of the bus starts listening.
paragraphs: The 9 Ashland bus was crawling north in the rain. Maria Ortega had taught the third-grade class at her parish that morning, and now she was riding home with her nephew Danny, who was thirteen and staring at a dead phone. "Tell me something," he said, mostly to pass the time. Maria thought for a moment. "Okay. A guy gets jumped on his way home from work. They take his wallet, his coat, his shoes, and leave him on the sidewalk. It is cold. He cannot get up."

Danny looked up. "Is this a real story?" "It is a story Jesus told," Maria said. "He told it about a road between two cities, but it works on any road. So the first person who walks by is a priest. Big deal in his community. He sees the man and crosses the street. The second person works at the Temple too, a Levite. He sees the man and keeps walking. Maybe they were late. Maybe they were scared."

"Then a third guy comes by, and this is the part that would have made people mad. He is a Samaritan." Danny shrugged. "Okay, it is like this," Maria said. "Picture the person your family argues about at Thanksgiving. The neighbor nobody trusts. The fan of the team you cannot stand. That guy. He stops. He cleans the wounds, puts the man in his own car, drives him to a motel, and pays for two nights. He tells the clerk he will cover anything else."

A woman across the aisle had stopped scrolling. A man in a Bears cap was nodding. "So Jesus turns to the lawyer who asked him the question," Maria said, "and asks him: which of those three was a neighbor to the man on the sidewalk? And the lawyer cannot even say the word Samaritan. He just says, the one who showed mercy. And Jesus says, go and do the same."

Danny was quiet for a block. "Why not just say be nice to people?" he asked. Maria smiled. "Because you would forget that by Fullerton. You will not forget the guy who crossed the street." The bus hissed to a stop. In a classroom, a scholar would call what Maria had just done a retelling of a parable in Luke's Gospel, chapter 10. On the bus, it was just a story that made strangers look up.
story.think: Maria changed the road, the coat and the motel, but kept the three travelers and the final question. What did the retelling keep that mattered most, and what might it have lost?

lessons.title: Judea Under Roman Rule
lessons.mainIdea: The Gospels are set in a Jewish land ruled by Rome, and that fact shapes almost every scene in them.
reading: In the Gospel of Luke, chapter 3, the writer dates the start of the story like a historian. He names the Roman emperor Tiberius, the governor Pontius Pilate, and a local ruler named Herod. That sentence tells a reader where the story sits. *Judea*, the region around Jerusalem, had come under Roman power when the general Pompey entered the city in 63 BCE. Rome ruled it first through a client king and then directly through governors.

The client king was Herod the Great, who ruled from 37 to 4 BCE. He rebuilt the Temple in Jerusalem on a grand scale and built the port city of Caesarea. After he died, his kingdom was split among his sons. In 6 CE Rome removed one son and placed Judea under its own officials. Galilee, in the north, stayed under Herod Antipas, another son. Pontius Pilate, a Roman *prefect*, governed Judea from about 26 to 36 CE. A stone found at Caesarea in 1961 carries his name and title.

Roman rule meant Roman taxes, Roman soldiers and Roman law. Tax collectors, called publicans in older English Bibles, were often local men who worked for the empire and were widely disliked. Several Gospel scenes turn on this: Jesus eats with tax collectors, and people object. Everyday people spoke *Aramaic*, a language close to Hebrew. Greek was the shared language of trade across the eastern empire, and the Gospels themselves were written in Greek. Hebrew was the language of scripture and prayer.

For readers today, this background matters. When a Gospel mentions a centurion, a coin with Caesar's face, or a cross, it is describing Roman power. In Roman Judea, crucifixion was a Roman punishment, used especially for slaves and rebels. Christians read these details as the setting for what they believe was a saving event. Historians read them as evidence for how a small Jewish movement began inside a large empire. Both kinds of readers need the same facts about the place and the time.

words.d: the region around Jerusalem in the southern part of the land; a Roman province from 6 CE
a Roman official who governed a province; Pontius Pilate held this title in Judea
the everyday language of Jews in Galilee and Judea in the first century, related to Hebrew
an older English word for a tax collector working for the Roman government

look.title: Roman Judea: Key Dates
rows: Roman army destroys the Jerusalem Temple
look.cite: Dates from the Roman historian Tacitus, the Jewish historian Josephus and standard reference works
look.prompt: Most scholars place the crucifixion around 30 to 33 CE. Which of these events happened before it, and which came after? Why might the events after it still matter for how the Gospels were written?

check.q: What was Pontius Pilate's role in Judea?
choices: The Roman official who governed the province
The Jewish high priest in charge of the Temple
The king who rebuilt the Temple
A tax collector who followed Jesus
check.why: Pilate was the Roman prefect, or governor, of Judea from about 26 to 36 CE. Herod the Great was the king who rebuilt the Temple.

check.q: Which language did most people in Galilee and Judea speak in daily life?
check.why: Aramaic, a language close to Hebrew, was the everyday spoken language. Greek was used for trade, and the Gospels were written in Greek.

check.q: Why do the Gospels' mentions of a centurion or a cross point to Rome?
choices: Because Rome had already left Judea
Because the Temple was built by Romans
Because soldiers and crucifixion were parts of Roman rule
Because the Gospels were written in Latin
check.why: Centurions commanded Roman soldiers, and crucifixion was a Roman punishment. Both details show the empire's power in the story's setting.

lessons.title: Temple, Synagogue and Rival Groups
lessons.mainIdea: First-century Judaism was varied, and the Gospels show Jesus in conversation and debate with several of its groups.
reading: Picture the Temple in Jerusalem around the year 30. Herod's builders had made it one of the largest sacred complexes in the Roman world. Priests offered daily sacrifices there, and Jewish pilgrims came from across the empire for the great festivals, especially Passover. Outside Jerusalem, Jews gathered in a local *synagogue* to read the Torah and pray. The Gospels show Jesus teaching in synagogues in Galilee and visiting the Temple at festival time.

The Jewish historian Josephus, writing later in the first century, described several groups within Judaism. The *Pharisees* were teachers who took the written Torah seriously and also followed oral traditions about how to keep it. They believed in the resurrection of the dead and were popular with ordinary people. The *Sadducees* were linked to the priestly families and the Temple. They accepted only the written Torah and did not believe in resurrection. A third group, the Essenes, lived apart in strict communities. Many scholars connect them with the Dead Sea Scrolls found near Qumran.

There were also people who wanted to fight Rome. By the time of the revolt in 66 CE, an armed group known as the Zealots was active. The *Samaritans* were not a Jewish group at all but a related people living between Galilee and Judea. They kept their own version of the Torah and worshiped on Mount Gerizim, not in Jerusalem. Jews and Samaritans generally avoided each other. That hostility is the background of the story Maria told on the bus.

The Gospels present Jesus arguing most often with Pharisees and scribes, but the arguments are inside Judaism, about how to keep the Sabbath, what makes a person clean, and which commandment is greatest. Modern scholars, Jewish and Christian, note that Jesus and the Pharisees shared much, including belief in resurrection. Reading these debates as one Jew talking with other Jews, rather than as Jesus against Judaism, is the approach most historians take today. It also helps avoid a long history of misreading.

words.d: a local Jewish house of gathering for prayer, Torah reading and teaching
first-century Jewish teachers who kept the written Torah along with oral traditions and believed in resurrection
a first-century Jewish group tied to the priests and the Temple that accepted only the written Torah
a people related to the Jews who kept their own Torah and worshiped on Mount Gerizim

look.title: Two Groups, One Question
look.text: In Mark, chapter 12, some Sadducees ask Jesus a puzzle about a woman who married seven brothers in turn: whose wife will she be in the resurrection? Jesus answers that they misunderstand both the scriptures and the power of God. Remember that Sadducees did not believe in resurrection, while Pharisees did.
look.prompt: Why would Sadducees, rather than Pharisees, ask this question? What does the scene tell you about how the Gospel writer wanted readers to see Jesus among the groups of his day?

check.q: Which group accepted only the written Torah and did not believe in resurrection?
check.why: Josephus and the Gospels both describe the Sadducees, tied to the Temple priests, as rejecting resurrection. The Pharisees accepted it.

check.q: Where did the Samaritans worship instead of the Jerusalem Temple?
check.why: The Samaritans kept their own Torah and held Mount Gerizim sacred. Qumran is linked to the Essenes, and Caesarea was Herod's port city.

check.q: How do most historians today describe the Gospel debates between Jesus and the Pharisees?
choices: As proof that Jesus rejected Judaism
As arguments within Judaism about how to keep the law
check.why: The debates concern the Sabbath, purity and the greatest commandment. Scholars read them as one Jew arguing with other Jews about shared scripture.

lessons.title: What a Gospel Is
lessons.mainIdea: A Gospel is an ancient account of Jesus written to proclaim good news, not a modern biography, and knowing that changes how you read it.
reading: Open the Gospel of Luke and you find a preface, one long sentence addressed to a man named Theophilus. The writer says that many have already tried to set down an account, that he has followed everything carefully from the beginning, and that he writes so that Theophilus may know the certainty of what he was taught. That is a clue to the *genre*. This is not a diary or a court record. It is a carefully arranged account with a purpose.

The word *gospel* comes from an Old English word meaning good news, which translates the Greek word euangelion. Mark opens with it: the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ. The four books we call Gospels were written in Greek, in the second half of the first century. Most scholars date Mark to around 70 CE, Matthew and Luke to the 80s, and John to the 90s, though these dates are estimates and debated. That places them roughly forty to sixty-five years after the events they describe.

In those decades the stories about Jesus were passed along by word of mouth, in preaching and teaching. Scholars call this *oral tradition*. The books do not name their authors inside the text. The names Matthew, Mark, Luke and John come from church tradition in the second century. Christians hold that the Gospels faithfully preserve what Jesus said and did. Historians study how the stories were shaped as they were told and written. A student in a public school learns to do the second while respecting the first.

The Gospels resemble ancient biographies of famous teachers in some ways: they focus on a person's deeds and sayings and devote much space to his death. But they also announce something. John states his purpose directly near the end: these things are written so that readers may believe. Reading a Gospel well means asking the questions from unit 13. Who wrote this, for whom, when and why? Those questions do not settle whether the message is true. They do tell you what kind of book you are holding.

words.d: good news; also one of the four New Testament books about the life, death and resurrection of Jesus
a kind of writing, such as letter, law, poetry or biography, with its own rules for how to read it
stories and teachings passed on by speaking and memory before they were written down

look.title: When Were the Gospels Written?
look.cite: Common scholarly estimates; exact dates are debated, and some scholars argue for earlier ones
look.prompt: If the crucifixion happened around 30 CE, about how many years passed before the first Gospel was written? What would have carried the stories in the meantime?

check.q: What does the Greek word euangelion mean?
check.why: Euangelion means good news, which the Old English word gospel translates. Mark's opening line uses it.

check.q: According to most scholars, which Gospel was written first?
check.why: Most scholars date Mark to around 70 CE, before Matthew, Luke and John, though the dates are debated.

check.q: Where do the names Matthew, Mark, Luke and John come from?
choices: Church tradition in the second century, since the books do not name their authors
Signatures at the end of each book
check.why: The Gospels are anonymous in the text. The traditional names were attached by early Christian writers in the second century.

lessons.title: The Three Synoptic Gospels
lessons.mainIdea: Matthew, Mark and Luke share so much material that they can be read side by side, yet each has its own emphasis.
reading: Lay Matthew, Mark and Luke in three columns and read the story of the paralyzed man carried to Jesus by his friends. The same scene appears in all three, often in the same words and the same order. Scholars call these three the *Synoptic* Gospels, from a Greek word meaning seen together. Most explain the overlap this way: Mark was written first, and Matthew and Luke each used Mark as a source, adding material of their own.

Matthew and Luke also share about two hundred verses that are not in Mark, mostly sayings of Jesus, such as much of the Sermon on the Mount. Many scholars think these came from a lost written collection they call Q, the *Q source*, from the German word Quelle, meaning source. Others think Luke used Matthew directly. No copy of Q has ever been found, so it remains a scholarly theory, though a widely held one.

Each Synoptic writer has a voice. Mark is the shortest, only sixteen chapters, and moves fast; the word immediately appears again and again. Mark stresses Jesus' suffering and the disciples' failure to understand. Matthew opens with a family tree reaching back to Abraham and quotes the Hebrew scriptures often to show what Christians believe was fulfilled. It groups Jesus' teaching into five long speeches. Luke, who also wrote Acts, gives special attention to the poor, to women, to outsiders and to prayer. Only Luke has the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son.

Reading synoptically means noticing the differences, not smoothing them out. Matthew's Beatitudes say blessed are the poor in spirit; Luke's say blessed are the poor. Christians have read both as true and complementary. Historians ask what each writer wanted his readers to hear. Either way, the comparison teaches a reading skill from unit 13: the same event told by two authors for two audiences will be told two ways.

words.d: seen together; the name for Matthew, Mark and Luke, which share much of the same material
a proposed lost collection of Jesus' sayings that many scholars think Matthew and Luke both used
the blessings that open the Sermon on the Mount, each beginning with the word blessed

look.title: Length of the Four Gospels
look.cite: Standard chapter divisions, added to the Bible in the thirteenth century
look.prompt: Mark is the shortest by far. If Matthew and Luke used Mark and added material, what kinds of material would you expect to find in them that Mark lacks?

check.q: Why are Matthew, Mark and Luke called Synoptic?
choices: They were all written by one author
They share so much material they can be read side by side
They are the three longest books in the Bible
check.why: Synoptic means seen together. The three share many of the same stories, often in the same words and order.

check.q: What is Q, in the study of the Gospels?
choices: A proposed lost source of sayings used by Matthew and Luke
A fifth Gospel found near Qumran
check.why: Q, from the German Quelle, is a scholarly theory about a lost sayings collection. No copy has been found.

check.q: Which Gospel alone contains the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son?
check.why: Both parables appear only in Luke, which pays special attention to outsiders, the poor and mercy.

lessons.title: John's Different Voice
lessons.mainIdea: The Gospel of John tells the story in its own order and language, presenting Jesus as the eternal Word made flesh.
reading: The Gospel of John does not begin in Bethlehem or at the Jordan River. It begins before creation. In the beginning was the Word, it says, echoing the first words of Genesis. Christians read this opening as a statement that Jesus existed with God before the world was made and then, as the text says, became flesh and dwelt among us. The Greek word for Word here is *Logos*, a term Greek thinkers used for the reason that orders the universe.

John's differences from the Synoptics are large. There are no parables in the Synoptic style and no Sermon on the Mount. Instead Jesus speaks in long conversations and speeches. He makes a series of *I am* statements: the bread of life, the light of the world, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life. John calls Jesus' miracles *signs*, and readers often count seven of them, including turning water into wine at Cana and raising Lazarus. In John, Jesus goes to Jerusalem several times, and the cleansing of the Temple comes near the start rather than the end.

John also tells the reader why he wrote. Near the end, in chapter 20, he says the signs were written so that readers may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name. That sentence is a plain statement of purpose. Most scholars date John to the 90s CE and see in it a community reflecting for decades on who Jesus was. Christians across traditions treasure John for its theology; the opening verses are read at Christmas in many churches.

For a comparative reader, John is a lesson in how one tradition can hold four accounts at once. The early church chose to keep all four rather than blend them into one. Around 180 CE the bishop Irenaeus argued that there should be exactly four Gospels, as there are four winds. The differences were not hidden. They were kept, and readers were expected to hold them together.

words.d: Greek for word or reason; John uses it for Jesus as God's Word present from the beginning
a series of statements in John in which Jesus describes himself, such as the light of the world
John's term for the miracles of Jesus, which the Gospel presents as pointing to who he is

look.title: John's Opening Line
look.text: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
look.cite: Gospel of John 1:1, King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Compare this opening with Genesis 1:1, which begins in the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. What is John doing by echoing those words, and how would a Christian reader hear it?

check.q: What does the Greek word Logos mean in John's opening?
check.why: Logos means word or reason. John uses it to present Jesus as God's Word present from the beginning.

check.q: What does John call the miracles of Jesus?
check.why: John uses the term signs for Jesus' miracles, presenting each as pointing to who he is.

check.q: According to John 20, why was the Gospel written?
choices: To replace the other three Gospels
So that readers may believe Jesus is the Christ and have life
check.why: John states his purpose directly: the signs are written so readers may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.

lessons.title: Teacher and Healer in Galilee
lessons.mainIdea: The Gospels present Jesus as a traveling teacher and healer in Galilee who gathered disciples and drew crowds.
reading: In Luke, chapter 4, Jesus stands up in the synagogue at Nazareth, his hometown, and reads from the scroll of Isaiah. The passage speaks of good news to the poor, freedom for captives and sight for the blind. Then he sits down and says that the scripture is fulfilled that day. Luke places this scene at the start of Jesus' public work. It sets a pattern: teaching in synagogues, quoting Israel's scriptures, and claiming that something long awaited is happening.

The Synoptics center that work in *Galilee*, the northern region of farms, hills and fishing towns around a large lake. Capernaum, a lakeside town, serves as a base. Jesus calls followers. Each *disciple*, or student, leaves work behind to follow a teacher. The first are fishermen: Simon, later called Peter, his brother Andrew, and the brothers James and John. Matthew, also called Levi, is a tax collector. From a larger group he chooses twelve, a number that echoes the twelve tribes of Israel.

Healing fills the early chapters of Mark. In Mark 2, four men carry a paralyzed friend to a crowded house, cannot get in, and lower him through the roof. In Mark 5, a woman who has bled for twelve years touches Jesus' cloak in a crowd, and the daughter of a synagogue leader named Jairus is raised. Christians believe each was a real *miracle* showing God's power. Historians note that the Jewish historian Josephus also described Jesus as a doer of remarkable deeds, and that the Gospels present each healing as a sign of the coming of God's rule.

Teaching and healing brought crowds and also conflict. Several stories involve the *Sabbath*, the weekly day of rest commanded in the Torah. Jesus heals on the Sabbath and defends it with an argument from scripture: the Sabbath was made for people, not people for the Sabbath. Some Pharisees objected. This was a live debate among Jewish teachers of the time about what work the Sabbath forbids. The Gospels show Jesus taking one side of it, not rejecting the day itself.

words.d: the northern region of hills, farms and fishing towns where the Gospels place most of Jesus' teaching
a student who follows a teacher; in the Gospels, one of Jesus' followers
an act that believers understand as showing God's power directly, such as a healing
the weekly day of rest, from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset, commanded in the Torah

look.title: Reading Isaiah in Nazareth
look.text: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised,
look.cite: Gospel of Luke 4:18, King James Version (1611); Jesus reads from Isaiah 61
look.prompt: Luke puts this reading at the start of Jesus' public work. Which groups of people does the passage name? What does that choice tell you about how Luke wants readers to understand Jesus' mission?

check.q: In Luke 4, what does Jesus read aloud in the synagogue at Nazareth?
choices: A passage from the scroll of Isaiah
check.why: Luke has Jesus read from Isaiah about good news to the poor and then announce that the scripture is fulfilled.

check.q: What was the work of the first disciples Jesus called?
check.why: Simon Peter, Andrew, James and John were fishermen on the lake of Galilee. Matthew, called later, was a tax collector.

check.q: What does the Sabbath argument in the Gospels show, according to the reading?
choices: That Jesus rejected the Sabbath entirely
That Jesus took one side in a Jewish debate about what work the Sabbath forbids
That the Sabbath was a Roman holiday
That only Sadducees kept the Sabbath
check.why: The Gospels present Jesus defending Sabbath healing from scripture, taking a position within a live debate among Jewish teachers.

lessons.title: The Sermon on the Mount
lessons.mainIdea: Matthew gathers Jesus' core moral teaching into one long speech that Christians have read as the heart of his ethics.
reading: Matthew, chapters 5 through 7, presents Jesus going up a mountain, sitting down as a teacher would, and speaking to his disciples with a crowd listening. Christians call this the *Sermon on the Mount*. It opens with the Beatitudes: blessed are the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the meek, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and those persecuted for doing right. Each blessing names a group the world tends to overlook and promises a reward, beginning and ending with the kingdom of heaven.

Then come six sayings built on a pattern: you have heard that it was said, but I say to you. Each takes a commandment from the Torah and pushes it inward. Do not murder becomes do not nurse anger. Love your neighbor becomes love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you. Jesus says he has come not to destroy the law but to fulfill it. Jewish and Christian scholars note that other Jewish teachers of the period also taught intention and mercy; the sermon's demands are intense, but its roots are in the Torah.

The middle of the sermon holds the *Lord's Prayer*, which Christians of nearly every branch recite. It addresses God as our Father. It asks that God's name be honored and God's kingdom come. Then it asks for daily bread, for forgiveness as we forgive others, and for rescue from evil. The sermon also warns against practicing piety to be seen, against storing up treasure on earth, and against judging others. Near the end comes the *Golden Rule*: do to others whatever you would have them do to you, which Matthew says sums up the law and the prophets.

Luke has a shorter parallel, the Sermon on the Plain in chapter 6, where the blessings are blunter, blessed are you poor, and are paired with woes to the rich. Readers have long debated how to live the sermon. Some Christians have read it as a rule for all believers, others as an ideal that shows human need for grace, others as a rule for a special few. The Hindu leader Gandhi, who was not a Christian, said the sermon went straight to his heart. It has been read far beyond the church.

words.d: Jesus' long teaching speech in Matthew 5 to 7, containing the Beatitudes and the Lord's Prayer
the prayer Jesus teaches in Matthew 6, beginning our Father, recited by Christians of nearly all branches
do to others what you would have them do to you; Matthew 7:12 says it sums up the law and the prophets

look.title: Love Your Enemies
look.text: But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;
look.cite: Gospel of Matthew 5:44, King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: The verse gives four actions, not just a feeling. List them. Why might a teacher spell out actions instead of saying only to feel love? How would you test whether someone was following this teaching?

check.q: What are the Beatitudes?
choices: The six sayings that begin you have heard that it was said
The blessings that open the Sermon on the Mount
check.why: The Beatitudes are the blessings in Matthew 5 that name groups such as the meek and the peacemakers and promise them a reward.

check.q: How does the sermon treat the Torah's commandments, according to the reading?
choices: It replaces them with Roman law
It pushes them inward toward intention, saying Jesus came to fulfill the law
check.why: The you have heard sayings take commandments and extend them to anger and to love of enemies. Jesus says he came to fulfill, not destroy, the law.

check.q: Which Gospel has a parallel speech called the Sermon on the Plain?
check.why: Luke 6 contains the Sermon on the Plain, with blunter blessings on the poor and woes on the rich.

lessons.title: The Good Samaritan
lessons.mainIdea: A parable is a short story that makes the listener answer a question, and the Good Samaritan turns who is my neighbor into who acted as one.
reading: A *parable* is a brief story drawn from ordinary life, a farmer, a lost coin, a wedding, that carries a meaning beyond itself and asks the hearer to respond. Jewish teachers of the period used parables, and the Synoptic Gospels record dozens from Jesus. They are not fables with a moral tacked on. They usually end with a twist or a question that leaves the hearer to decide. The Good Samaritan, in Luke 10, is the best-known example.

Luke frames it with a conversation. A scholar of the law asks what he must do to inherit eternal life. Jesus asks him what the law says, and he answers by joining two commands from the Torah: love God with all your heart, from Deuteronomy, and love your *neighbor* as yourself, from Leviticus. Jesus approves. Then the man asks, and who is my neighbor? That question is about limits. Where does my duty stop? The parable is the answer.

A man traveling from Jerusalem down to Jericho is beaten and left half dead. A priest sees him and passes on the other side; so does a Levite, a member of the tribe that served in the Temple. Then a Samaritan comes, feels *compassion*, bandages his wounds with oil and wine, sets him on his own animal, brings him to an inn, and pays the innkeeper two silver coins with a promise to cover more. For Luke's first hearers, the shock was the hero's identity. Samaritans and Jews were hostile neighbors, as the previous lesson explained.

Jesus then reverses the question. He does not ask who counts as the wounded man's neighbor. He asks which of the three was a neighbor to him. The scholar answers, the one who showed mercy, and Jesus says, go and do likewise. Christians have read the story as a call to love without limits, and some early readers also read it as an allegory of Christ rescuing humanity. Either way, notice the method: the story makes the listener give the answer he did not want to give.

words.d: a short story from everyday life that carries a deeper meaning and asks the hearer to respond
in Leviticus 19:18, the person one is commanded to love as oneself; the parable asks who that includes
being moved by another person's suffering and acting to help; the Samaritan's response in the story

look.title: The Question Turned Around
look.text: Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves? And he said, He that shewed mercy on him. Then said Jesus unto him, Go, and do thou likewise.
look.cite: Gospel of Luke 10:36-37, King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: The scholar asked who is my neighbor. Jesus asks who was a neighbor. Explain the difference between the two questions in your own words. Why might the scholar avoid saying the word Samaritan?

check.q: What two commands does the law scholar join together in Luke 10?
choices: Keep the Sabbath and honor your parents
Love God with all your heart and love your neighbor as yourself
Do not steal and do not murder
check.why: He quotes Deuteronomy on loving God and Leviticus 19:18 on loving one's neighbor, and Jesus approves the answer.

check.q: Why was the identity of the hero shocking to Luke's first hearers?
choices: Because he was a Roman soldier
Because Samaritans and Jews were hostile to each other
Because he was the wounded man's brother
check.why: Jews and Samaritans avoided each other. Making the Samaritan the one who shows mercy overturns the hearers' expectations.

check.q: How does Jesus change the scholar's question at the end of the parable?
choices: He asks how much the inn cost
He asks why the priest was late
He asks whether Samaritans can be saved
He asks which traveler acted as a neighbor instead of who counts as one
check.why: The scholar asked about the limits of who is a neighbor. Jesus asks who behaved as a neighbor, shifting the focus to action.

lessons.title: The Prodigal Son and the Sower
lessons.mainIdea: Parables about a lost son and a scattering farmer show how these stories work on hearers and why they are read in more than one way.
reading: Luke 15 opens with a complaint: Pharisees and scribes grumble that Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them. Luke answers with three parables about lost things, a sheep, a coin and a son. In the third, a younger son demands his share of the inheritance early, travels to a far country, wastes everything, and ends up feeding pigs during a famine. He comes to himself and heads home, rehearsing an apology. Older English Bibles call him the *prodigal*, meaning wasteful.

Before he can finish speaking, his father sees him from far off, runs to him, embraces him, and calls for a robe, a ring and a feast. The elder brother, who stayed and worked, refuses to come in. The father goes out to him too and says: you are always with me, but your brother was dead and is alive again. The story ends without telling us whether the elder brother goes in. That open ending is the point. The hearers who grumbled are left to decide what they will do.

The Sower, in Mark 4, works differently. A farmer scatters seed. Some falls on the path and birds eat it; some on rocky ground, where it sprouts fast and withers; some among thorns, which choke it; some on good soil, where it yields thirty, sixty and a hundred times over. Mark then has Jesus explain it privately: the seed is the word, and the soils are kinds of hearers. Scholars note this is one of the few parables the Gospels themselves interpret, as an *allegory* in which each part stands for something.

These two parables show the range of the form. One is a family drama with no explanation; the other is a picture with a key attached. Christians have read the Prodigal Son as a portrait of God's forgiveness, and preachers have asked which brother the listener resembles. The Sower has been read as encouragement to keep preaching despite failure. Rembrandt painted the father's embrace; the story has shaped art and music far beyond the church. To read a parable, ask who is listening in the story and what the ending leaves open.

words.d: recklessly wasteful; the traditional name for the younger son in Luke 15
a story in which each part stands for something else, as the soils in the Sower stand for kinds of hearers
property passed from parents to children, usually after death; the younger son asks for his early

look.title: Two Endings
look.text: The Prodigal Son ends with the father pleading outside the feast and the elder brother's answer left unsaid. The Sower ends with a full explanation of what every soil means. Luke tells the first to grumbling critics; Mark says Jesus explained the second only to his disciples in private.
look.prompt: Why might one parable be left open and the other explained? Think about who is listening in each case. Which kind of story do you find stays with you longer, and why?

check.q: What prompts the three parables of lost things in Luke 15?
choices: A complaint that Jesus eats with sinners
check.why: Luke 15 opens with Pharisees and scribes grumbling that Jesus welcomes sinners. The parables answer that complaint.

check.q: What is unusual about the Sower compared with most parables?
choices: It is told only in John
The Gospels themselves explain what each part means
check.why: Mark 4 has Jesus interpret the Sower privately: the seed is the word, the soils are kinds of hearers. Most parables are left unexplained.

check.q: How does the Prodigal Son end?
choices: The elder brother joins the feast
Without saying whether the elder brother goes in
check.why: The story stops with the father's plea. Its open ending leaves the grumbling hearers to decide their own response.

lessons.title: The Week of the Passion
lessons.mainIdea: All four Gospels slow down to tell the last week of Jesus' life in detail, from his entry into Jerusalem to his death on a Roman cross.
reading: Every Gospel gives a large share of its pages to one week. Christians call this the *Passion*, from a Latin word for suffering. It begins with Jesus entering Jerusalem at Passover time, riding a donkey while crowds spread branches and cloaks. Matthew links the scene to the prophet Zechariah's picture of a humble king. Jesus then overturns the tables of money changers in the Temple courts, an act that the Gospels present as angering the Temple authorities.

On the night before his death, the Synoptics describe a Passover meal with the twelve. Jesus breaks bread and shares a cup, saying this is my body and this is my blood of the covenant. Christians call this the *Last Supper*, and most churches repeat its words in worship as communion, the Eucharist or the Lord's Supper. Afterward, in a garden called Gethsemane, Jesus prays in distress. Judas, one of the twelve, arrives with an armed group, and Jesus is arrested.

The trials follow. Jesus is questioned before the high priest Caiaphas and a council, then handed to Pilate, the Roman governor. The Gospels and most historians hold that only the Roman governor could order an execution. The Gospels show him reluctant, offering to release a prisoner, but yielding to pressure. Historians stress that *crucifixion* was a Roman penalty, and that the charge written above Jesus' head, King of the Jews, was political. Roman soldiers carry out the sentence at a place called Golgotha outside the city wall, with two others crucified beside him.

Mark's account is stark. At the ninth hour Jesus cries out in Aramaic the first line of Psalm 22, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me, and dies. A member of the council named Joseph of Arimathea asks Pilate for the body and lays it in a rock-cut tomb before the Sabbath begins. Christians observe this week as Holy Week, with Palm Sunday, Holy Thursday and Good Friday. For centuries many Christians blamed the Jewish people as a whole for the death, a charge used to justify persecution. Many churches today, as in the Catholic declaration Nostra Aetate of 1965, reject that charge and stress that Rome carried out the execution.

words.d: from the Latin for suffering; the Christian name for Jesus' last days, arrest, trial and crucifixion
the final meal Jesus shared with his disciples, remembered by Christians in communion or the Eucharist
a Roman method of execution by nailing or tying a person to a cross, used for slaves and rebels
the week before Easter, when Christians remember the events from Palm Sunday to the crucifixion

look.title: A Psalm on the Cross
look.text: And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
look.cite: Gospel of Mark 15:34, King James Version (1611); the words are the opening of Psalm 22
look.prompt: Mark keeps the Aramaic words and then translates them. Why might he do that for Greek-speaking readers? Look up how Psalm 22 ends. How might knowing the whole psalm change the way a reader hears this cry?

check.q: Why did Jesus' case go to Pilate?
choices: Because Pilate was the high priest
Because Pilate had asked to meet Jesus
Because the Roman governor held the power to order an execution
check.why: The Gospels show a council questioning Jesus, but the death sentence and crucifixion were Roman, and Pilate held that authority.

check.q: What do Christians remember in communion, the Eucharist or the Lord's Supper?
choices: The Last Supper, when Jesus shared bread and a cup
The entry into Jerusalem on a donkey
The reading in the Nazareth synagogue
The feeding of the five thousand
check.why: At the Last Supper Jesus said this is my body and this is my blood of the covenant. Churches repeat those words in worship.

check.q: What does Jesus cry out in Mark's account of the crucifixion?
check.why: Mark 15:34 records Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani, the Aramaic opening of Psalm 22, my God, why have you forsaken me.

lessons.title: The Resurrection as Christians Believe It
lessons.mainIdea: The claim that Jesus rose from the dead is the center of Christian faith, told with an empty tomb and appearances in four differing accounts.
reading: Early on the first day of the week, according to Mark, three women went to the tomb with spices to anoint the body: Mary Magdalene, another Mary, and Salome. They found the stone rolled away and a young man in white who told them Jesus of Nazareth had been raised and was not there. Mark says they fled, trembling, and said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid. The oldest manuscripts of Mark end right there, at verse 8 of chapter 16. Longer endings were added later.

Matthew, Luke and John go on to describe appearances. Matthew has the risen Jesus meet the disciples on a mountain in Galilee and send them to all nations. Luke tells of two followers who walk to the village of Emmaus with a stranger and recognize him when he breaks bread. John describes Mary Magdalene meeting Jesus in the garden, and Thomas doubting until he sees the wounds. In every Gospel, women are the first at the tomb. The four accounts differ in details, and readers have compared them for centuries.

For Christians, the *resurrection* is not a detail but the foundation. Paul, writing to Corinth around 55 CE, before any Gospel was finished, passes on what he says he received: that Christ died, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Peter, to the twelve, and to many others. It is the earliest written list of those to whom Jesus appeared, and one of the earliest statements of the belief. Paul adds that if Christ was not raised, Christian preaching is empty. Christians hold that the resurrection shows God's victory over death and promises their own.

Historians work differently. They do not claim to prove or disprove a miracle. They can establish that the earliest followers believed Jesus had been raised, that the belief appeared within a few years of his death, and that it drove the movement's growth. Christians celebrate the resurrection every Sunday and above all at *Easter*, the oldest yearly Christian festival and, for most Christians, the most important. Most Orthodox churches calculate the date differently, so Easter often falls on different Sundays in Chicago's Greek Orthodox and Catholic churches.

words.d: rising from the dead; the Christian belief that God raised Jesus bodily on the third day
the yearly Christian festival of the resurrection, the oldest and central feast of the church year
a follower of Jesus from Magdala whom all four Gospels place at the empty tomb

look.title: Where Mark Stops
look.text: In the oldest copies, Mark ends with the women running from the tomb, afraid and silent. Matthew ends with the risen Jesus sending the disciples into the world. Luke ends with him blessing them and being taken up. John ends with a breakfast on the shore and a note that the world could not hold all the books that could be written.
look.prompt: Four endings, four moods. Why might Mark stop at fear and silence? What does each ending tell you about what its writer most wanted readers to carry away?

check.q: Who does every Gospel place first at the empty tomb?
check.why: All four Gospels name women, and always Mary Magdalene, as the first to find the tomb empty.

check.q: Which of these is the earliest written statement of the resurrection belief?
choices: Paul's letter to the Corinthians, around 55 CE
check.why: Paul's first letter to Corinth, written before any Gospel, passes on a tradition that Christ died, was buried, was raised and appeared.

check.q: What can historians establish about the resurrection, according to the reading?
choices: That the earliest followers believed it within a few years of Jesus' death
That the miracle certainly did not happen
That no one believed it until the fourth century
check.why: Historians do not rule on miracles. They can show that the belief arose very early and drove the movement's growth.

lessons.title: The Kingdom of God
lessons.mainIdea: The Gospels sum up Jesus' message as the kingdom of God, God's rule arriving now and still to come, which Christians pray for and interpret in several ways.
reading: Mark reports the first words of Jesus' preaching this way: the time is fulfilled, and the *kingdom of God* is at hand; repent, and believe the good news. That phrase runs through the Synoptic Gospels. It does not mean a place with borders. It means God's rule, God reigning as king over the world. Matthew usually says kingdom of heaven, meaning the same thing; many scholars explain this as a reverent Jewish habit of speaking of God indirectly. Jews of the time already hoped for God's rule; the Gospels announce that it is arriving in Jesus.

Many parables describe the kingdom. It is like a mustard seed, the smallest seed, that grows into a great shrub where birds nest. It is like yeast a woman hides in flour until the whole batch rises. It is like treasure found in a field, or a pearl worth selling everything for. The pictures share a pattern: something small and hidden, then something large and total. The kingdom belongs, Jesus says, to the poor, to children, and to those who become like them.

Is the kingdom now or later? The Gospels say both. Jesus tells people the kingdom is among them, and he also teaches them to pray thy kingdom come, in the Lord's Prayer. Scholars use the word *eschatology*, from a Greek word for last things, for teaching about the end and God's final purpose. Some emphasize that Jesus expected the end soon; others that he saw God's rule already present in his healings and meals. Most now say the Gospels hold the two together: begun, not finished.

Christians have drawn different conclusions. Some have understood the kingdom mainly as heaven after death. Others, including many in the Social Gospel movement in American cities like Chicago around 1900, understood it as a call to remake society with justice now. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant teaching all include both dimensions in some form. A comparative reader can note that this question, how God's purpose meets human history, appears in Judaism and Islam too, each with its own answer.

words.d: God's rule or reign over the world; the central theme of Jesus' preaching in the Synoptic Gospels
teaching about last things, the end of history and God's final purpose
to turn around, change one's mind and way of life; Mark pairs it with believing the good news

look.title: Small Seed, Great Shrub
look.text: Jesus says the kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man plants in his field. It is the smallest of seeds, but when grown it is larger than the garden plants and becomes a tree where birds come to nest. Matthew places this beside a second picture: yeast a woman hides in three measures of flour until all of it is leavened.
look.prompt: Both pictures start with something tiny and hidden. What is each one saying about how God's rule arrives? Why might a teacher choose a seed and bread dough instead of an army or a throne?

check.q: What does the phrase kingdom of God mean in the Gospels?
choices: God's rule or reign over the world
check.why: The kingdom is God reigning as king, not a place with borders. Matthew's kingdom of heaven means the same thing.

check.q: Why does Matthew usually say kingdom of heaven instead of kingdom of God?
choices: Because Matthew was written in Latin
Because Matthew describes a different kingdom
Many scholars think it reflects a reverent Jewish habit of speaking of God indirectly
Because the phrase came from Roman law
check.why: Many scholars think Matthew followed a reverent Jewish habit of speaking of God indirectly, using heaven in place of God. The meaning is the same.

check.q: According to most scholars, is the kingdom present or future in the Gospels?
choices: Both begun and still to come
check.why: Jesus says the kingdom is among people and also teaches them to pray for it to come. Scholars describe it as begun but not finished.

review.q: Which statement about Judea in the time of Jesus is correct?
choices: It was a Roman province governed by a prefect
It was an independent kingdom with no Roman presence
It was ruled directly by the emperor living in Jerusalem
review.why: From 6 CE Rome ruled Judea through its own officials. Pontius Pilate was prefect from about 26 to 36 CE.

review.q: What do scholars mean when they call Matthew, Mark and Luke the Synoptic Gospels?
choices: They were written at the same time
They share much material and can be read side by side
They were all written by disciples
review.why: Synoptic means seen together. The three overlap heavily, and most scholars think Matthew and Luke used Mark as a source.

review.q: Which of these appears in John but not in the Synoptic Gospels?
choices: The opening about the Word who was with God
The Last Supper words this is my body
review.why: John opens with the Logos, the Word made flesh. The Sermon on the Mount and the Sower are Synoptic material.

review.q: In the Good Samaritan, what does Jesus do with the question who is my neighbor?
choices: He answers that only fellow Jews are neighbors
He says the question does not matter
He tells the scholar to ask a priest
He turns it into which traveler acted as a neighbor
review.why: Luke 10:36 has Jesus ask which of the three was neighbor to the wounded man, shifting the question from limits to action.

review.q: What is the Golden Rule as Matthew states it?
choices: Do to others what you would have them do to you
Love the Lord your God with all your heart
review.why: Matthew 7:12 gives the Golden Rule and says it sums up the law and the prophets. The others are different sayings.

review.q: Why do historians stress that crucifixion was a Roman punishment?
choices: Because Jewish courts used it often
Because it shows Rome carried out the execution, not the Jewish people
Because it proves Jesus was a Roman citizen
review.why: Crucifixion was Rome's penalty for slaves and rebels. Stressing this counters centuries of blaming Jews for Jesus' death.

review.q: Which of these is the earliest written source for the belief that Jesus rose from the dead?
choices: Paul's first letter to the Corinthians
review.why: Paul wrote to Corinth around 55 CE, passing on a tradition about Christ's death, burial, resurrection and appearances, before any Gospel.

review.q: Which best describes the kingdom of God in the Synoptic Gospels?
choices: A political plan to overthrow Rome
The land of Israel restored to Herod
God's rule, already arriving and still to come
review.why: Jesus announces the kingdom is at hand, says it is among people, and teaches disciples to pray for it to come.
